q: You are anchoring on sand in 5 m. How do you let the chain go?
a: Pay it out as the boat drifts back
o: Drop it all at once in a heap
Pay it out while motoring ahead
Lower the anchor, keep the rest aboard
why: Laying the chain along the bottom as you move astern lets the anchor dig in.

q: You look down through clear water to pick a spot. Where do you drop the anchor?
a: A — on the sand
o: B — in the thick weed
C — on the flat rock
B — the weed cushions the chain
why: Sand gives good holding; anchors skate on weed and cannot dig into rock.

fig.note: Seen through clear water, depth 5–7 m

q: Going stern-to in a marina, your crew pick up the lazy line at the stern. What do they do with it?
a: Walk it forward and cleat it at the bow
o: Cleat it at the stern with the stern line
Drop it once the stern lines are on
Hold it by hand until you leave
why: The lazy line replaces your anchor: lead it forward and cleat it tight at the bow.

q: The anchor is down and the chain laid out. How do you make sure it is holding?
a: Go astern gently, then harder, watching a transit
o: Wait — it will dig in by itself overnight
Motor ahead over it to press it in
Jerk the chain by hand at the bow
why: Set the anchor with steady astern power; a fixed transit ashore shows if you are moving.

q: You are going stern-to here. Where do you let go the anchor?
a: About 3–4 boat lengths off the quay
o: About one boat length off the quay
About half a length off the quay
About ten boat lengths off the quay
why: Three to four lengths out leaves enough chain on the bottom to hold you off the quay.

q: Reversing stern-to the quay with your anchor down, when do you take the chain up tight?
a: Once the stern lines are made fast
o: As soon as the anchor hits the bottom
Before the crew throw the stern lines
Only if the wind gets up overnight
why: Pay out freely while reversing; with the stern lines on, tighten the chain to hold you off.

q: Leaving the quay in the morning, your windlass lifts a neighbour's chain hooked over your anchor. What do you do?
a: Hold their chain on a line, lower yours clear
o: Motor hard ahead to drag both free
Keep winching until both anchors are up
Motor astern to pull yours out from under
why: Take the other chain's weight on a slip line, drop your anchor clear, then slip the line.

q: Lying alongside the town quay, the wash from passing boats makes you surge fore and aft. Which lines stop it?
a: The springs
o: The bow and stern lines
The breast lines
Extra fenders along the side
why: Springs run fore and aft along the quay and stop the boat surging forward and back.

q: You need to get the stern out first. How do you leave?
a: Ahead against a bow spring, bow fendered
o: Astern against a bow spring, bow fendered
Ahead against a stern spring, stern fendered
Push the stern off by hand, then go ahead
why: Motoring ahead against a spring from the bow pivots the bow in and swings the stern out.

fig.title: Alongside the quay
lines: Wind F4 pinning you onto the quay

q: You choose a spot for the night. Where do you anchor?
a: B — in the lee, south of the island
o: A — close under the north shore
C — off the west end, in open water
A — the wind will hold you off the shore
why: Anchor in the lee of the land; a north wind blows onto the north shore and across open water.

q: Is this a good place to drop your anchor?
a: No — your swinging circles overlap
o: Yes — boats on chain swing together
Yes — 30 m is more than your length
Yes, if you lay less chain to fit
why: In shifting wind boats swing differently; leave room for both swinging circles.

fig.title: Crowded bay, Sivota
lines: Depth 5 m, you plan 25 m of chain

q: What is happening, and what do you do?
a: You are dragging — start the engine
o: You are swinging — go back to bed
The GPS lost its fix — reset it
The alarm radius is small — enlarge it
why: A straight track downwind away from the swinging arcs means the anchor is dragging.

fig.title: 02:30 at anchor
lines: Track: arcs, then a line downwind

q: How do you lie here for the night?
a: Anchor out, stern line to a rock or tree
o: Anchor in the middle on a long scope
Bow line to a tree, no anchor at all
Two anchors off the bow, no line ashore
why: In a narrow cove, anchor and take a stern line ashore so the boat cannot swing.

fig.title: Narrow cove, Turkey
lines: Too narrow to swing at anchor

q: Leaving the anchorage, your crew start the windlass. How do you help them?
a: Motor gently towards the anchor as they signal
o: Let the windlass pull the boat up to it
Motor astern to keep the chain tight
Motor hard ahead to break it out first
why: Motor slowly up to the chain as the crew point; a windlass is not built to haul the boat.

q: Leaving a lazy-line berth, how do you handle the lazy line?
a: Drop it at the bow and let it sink first
o: Drop it over the stern as you go ahead
Keep it aboard until clear of the berth
Lead it aft and hand it to the quay
why: Let the lazy line sink clear before you motor ahead, or it can wrap round the propeller.

q: You wake to find this. What do you do?
a: Tighten the chain and ease the stern lines
o: Tighten the stern lines to hold her in
Ease the chain so she can ride it out
Add a fender and leave the lines alone
why: Bring in chain to pull the stern off the quay, easing the stern lines to match.

fig.title: Stern-to, 03:00
lines: Wind has swung onto the quay, F5
Stern now 0.5 m from the stone

q: Where do you anchor?
a: B — about 6 m of water
o: A — about 25 m of water
C — about 2.2 m of water
A — well clear of the beach
why: 50 m of chain gives only 2:1 in 25 m; 2.2 m leaves no margin under a 1.9 m keel.

fig.note: You carry 50 m of chain, draft 1.9 m

q: You are going stern-to with a fresh wind blowing across the line of berths. Where do you drop the anchor?
a: A little upwind of the line of your berth
o: A little downwind of the line of your berth
Exactly in line, then reverse in harder
Close in, so the wind has less effect
why: The wind will sag the boat downwind, leaving the chain running straight out from your berth.

q: Where do you spend the night?
a: B — sheltered from the stronger southerly
o: A — it is sheltered from the wind now
A — the southerly will hold you off
Either — any anchor holds in F5
why: Pick shelter from the strongest forecast wind, not just the wind blowing now.

fig.title: Choosing tonight's cove
lines: Cove A: open to the south
Cove B: open to the north

q: What is the least chain you let out?
a: About 32 m
o: About 28 m
About 24 m
About 16 m
why: Measure from the bow roller: (7 m + 1 m) × 4 = 32 m.
